section.title: David Destroys the Amalekites
section.sectionRationale: This is David's darkest hour as a fugitive: Ziklag burned, both his wives and every family taken captive, and his own men speaking of stoning him. Yet in the ashes David turns to the LORD for strength and guidance, pursues, recovers everyone and everything, and then insists that the exhausted who stayed behind share equally in the spoil, a lasting statute of grace in Israel.
section.thesis: Stripped of home, family, and even the loyalty of his men, David does not collapse into despair or revenge; strengthened and guided by the LORD, he recovers all that was lost and freely shares it with the weary, showing that the true anointed king cares for the weak rather than only the strong.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: Ziklag in ashes and the threat of stoning; David inquires of the LORD and pursues; the Amalekites destroyed and everything recovered; the just sharing of the spoil; and gifts sent to the elders of Judah.

units.label: Ziklag in ashes
units.note: but David found strength in the LORD his God

verses.text: On the third day David and his men arrived in Ziklag, and the Amalekites had raided the Negev, attacked Ziklag, and burned it down.
They had taken captive the women and all who were there, both young and old. They had not killed anyone, but had carried them off as they went on their way.
When David and his men came to the city, they found it burned down and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive.
So David and the troops with him lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep.
David’s two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel, had been taken captive.
And David was greatly distressed because the people spoke of stoning him, because the soul of every man grieved for his sons and daughters. But David {{chazaq|found strength}} in the LORD his God.

units.label: David inquires of the LORD
units.note: the ephod, the answer, and the pursuit

verses.text: Then David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, “Bring me the ephod.” So Abiathar brought it to him,
and David {{darash|inquired}} of the LORD: “Should I pursue these raiders? Will I overtake them?” “Pursue them,” the LORD replied, “for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives.”
So David and his six hundred men went to the Brook of Besor, where some stayed behind
because two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook. But David and four hundred men continued in pursuit.
Now his men found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. They gave the man water to drink and food to eat,
a piece of a fig cake and two clusters of raisins. So he ate and was revived, for he had not had any food or water for three days and three nights.
Then David asked him, “To whom do you belong, and where are you from?” “I am an Egyptian,” he replied, “the slave of an Amalekite. My master abandoned me three days ago when I fell ill.
We raided the Negev of the Cherethites, the territory of Judah, and the Negev of Caleb, and we burned down Ziklag.”
“Will you lead me to these raiders?” David asked. And the man replied, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hand of my master, and I will lead you to them.”

units.label: Everything recovered
units.note: not a man escaped, nothing was missing

verses.text: So he led David down, and there were the Amalekites spread out over all the land, eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and the land of Judah.
And David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day. Not a man escaped, except four hundred young men who fled, riding off on camels.
So David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives.
Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder the Amalekites had taken. David brought everything back.
And he took all the flocks and herds, which his men drove ahead of the other livestock, calling out, “This is David’s plunder!”

units.label: Sharing the spoil
units.note: they will share alike, a statute in Israel

verses.text: When David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow him and who were left behind at the Brook of Besor, they came out to meet him and the troops with him. As David approached the men, he greeted them,

but all the wicked and worthless men among those who had gone with David said, “Because they did not go with us, we will not share with them the plunder we recovered, except for each man’s wife and children. They may take them and go.”
But David said, “My brothers, you must not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders who came against us.
Who will listen to your proposal? The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike.”
And so it has been from that day forward. David established this statute and ordinance for Israel to this very day.

units.label: Gifts to the elders of Judah
units.note: a gift from the plunder of the LORD's enemies

verses.text: When David arrived in Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying, “Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies.”
He sent gifts to those in Bethel, Ramoth Negev, and Jattir;
to those in Aroer, Siphmoth, and Eshtemoa;
to those in Racal and in the cities of the Jerahmeelites and Kenites;
to those in Hormah, Bor-ashan, and Athach;
and to those in Hebron and in all the places where David and his men had roamed.

chazaq.gloss: To strengthen, prevail, take hold firmly. In 30:6, at the point of total loss, threatened with stoning by his own grieving men, David strengthened himself, or found strength, in the LORD his God. It is not self-help but active reliance on God when every human support has failed.

darash.gloss: To inquire, seek, consult. In 30:8 David inquires of the LORD through the ephod before acting, seeking explicit direction rather than presuming or acting on emotion alone. The same deliberate seeking marks David throughout his fugitive years.

basic.context: David returns from being dismissed by the Philistine commanders to find Ziklag, his adopted home, burned to the ground by Amalekite raiders. His wives and the families of all six hundred men are gone. His own men, grief stricken, talk of stoning him. It is the lowest point in David's story: he has lost his home, his family, and even the loyalty of his followers. But instead of collapsing, David turns to God, inquires whether to pursue, receives a clear answer, and sets out. Along the way a half dead Egyptian slave becomes the key to finding the raiders. David destroys the Amalekite raiding party, recovers everyone and everything, and then, when some of his men want to exclude the exhausted two hundred who stayed behind from the plunder, David insists on equal sharing, making it a lasting statute in Israel.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing what David actually did; it is not a command that plunder must always be divided equally today. What carries forward is the pattern: when everything is lost and support crumbles, the godly response is to seek strength and guidance from the LORD rather than despair or vengeance, and true leadership shares grace with the weary rather than hoarding reward for the strong.
basic.originalLanguages: At the darkest moment David chazaq, strengthened himself, or found strength, in the LORD his God, turning to God rather than despair or self defense against his own men. He then darash, inquired, of the LORD through the ephod, asking plainly whether to pursue and waiting for an answer before acting. Seeking strength and seeking guidance go together: David does not presume on God's help, he asks for it, receives it, and only then moves.
basic.typology: David recovering all that was lost, and sharing it generously with those too weary to fight, anticipates the greater Son of David who loses nothing of what the Father has given him and freely shares the spoils of his victory with those who could not fight for themselves.
basic.christ: David, God's anointed but not yet crowned king, is stripped of home and family, then rises by God's strength to win back everything and share it as pure gift with the exhausted. This points forward to great David's greater Son, who was stripped of everything on the cross, was raised by the Father's power, and now freely shares the spoils of his victory, forgiveness, life, and an inheritance, with those too weak to have earned any part of it themselves.
basic.god: God does not prevent Ziklag from burning, but he meets David in the ashes: he is the God in whom the strengthless find strength, the God who answers when sought, and the God whose character of shared, undeserved grace becomes law through David's ruling, they will share alike.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 31 gives the Mosaic precedent for dividing plunder between those who fought and the rest of the congregation. Isaiah 40 promises strength to the weary who wait on the LORD. Psalm 18 is David's own testimony that the LORD is his strength. Matthew 20 pictures the same grace of reward given by the master's generosity rather than strictly by hours worked.
basic.oneStory: David's rock bottom moment, home burned, family gone, own men ready to stone him, becomes one of Scripture's clearest pictures of finding strength in God alone. His recovery of all that was lost, and his insistence on grace for the weary, is a small chapter in the long story of the God who restores what is lost and gives grace freely, a story that reaches its height in Christ, the true King who wins back everything sin destroyed and freely shares it with his people.

context.literary: The chapter is staged in five scenes, each marked by a shift in location or mood: catastrophe and near mutiny at the smoking ruins of Ziklag, verses 1 to 6; inquiry of the LORD and the pursuit itself, verses 7 to 15; the sudden reversal of fortune at the Amalekite camp, verses 16 to 20; the dispute over dividing the spoil, verses 21 to 25; and the closing notice of gifts sent to Judah's elders, verses 26 to 31. The turning point of the whole movement is a single half verse, but David found strength in the LORD his God, verse 6, placed exactly at the point of maximum despair, after the weeping has exhausted itself and before any plan has formed. Everything that follows, the request for the ephod, the LORD's direct answer, the discovery of the Egyptian, the total victory, flows from that one sentence. The narrator also builds a quiet contrast into the pacing: verses 1 to 6 move at the speed of grief, short clauses piling one on another, while verses 7 to 15 slow to a careful, procedural pace, inquiry, march, rest, discovery, questioning, oath, each step given its own verse. The effect mirrors David's own movement from panic to composed action. The final section, gifts distributed to a dozen or more named towns, verses 26 to 31, reads almost like a list, deliberately unglamorous, and quietly plants the political seeds for David's coronation over Judah in the very next book.
context.historical: Ziklag lay in the Negev, the arid southern borderlands between Judah and Philistine and Amalekite territory, granted to David by Achish as a base for his six hundred men and their households, 1 Samuel 27:6. Its exposed, undefended position, with David's entire fighting force away at the Philistine muster, 1 Samuel 29, made it an easy target the moment raiders watching from a distance realized the town stood empty of its men. The Amalekites were old enemies, first encountered ambushing Israel from the rear during the exodus, Deuteronomy 25:17-19, and marked out then for eventual destruction, a sentence Saul himself had been commanded, and had failed, to carry out fully in 1 Samuel 15. Their pattern here, raiding, burning, taking captives rather than killing them, matches the behavior of nomadic raiders throughout the ancient Near East who valued slaves and plunder over holding territory. The Brook of Besor, a seasonal wadi south of Ziklag, marks the limit of the exhausted men's endurance, and David's insistence that those who guarded the supplies there share equally with those who fought reflects a principle already present in Israel's law for holy war, Numbers 31:27, though David is the one who fixes it permanently as binding custom for Israel. The towns named in verses 27 to 31, scattered across Judah's Negev and hill country, were likely places David and his men had sheltered or received help during his fugitive years, so the gifts function as repayment as much as political preparation ahead of his anointing as king over Judah.
context.canonical: This chapter is David's last recorded act before news of Saul's death reaches him, and its placement is deliberate: immediately after being cleared of any complicity in Israel's defeat, chapter 29, David is shown doing exactly what a shepherd king should do, recovering the lost and sharing the spoils of victory generously, before any crown is even offered to him. The statute of equal sharing echoes, and formalizes, Moses' ruling that plunder be divided between those who fought and the rest of the congregation, Numbers 31:25-27; David does not invent the principle but extends it into permanent law, from that day forward, verse 25. The gifts to Judah's elders, verses 26-31, anticipate 2 Samuel 2:1-4, where the men of Judah anoint David king at Hebron, itself named among the towns that received a gift here. The Egyptian slave rescued half dead in the field, an outsider with no standing among either Israelites or Amalekites, becomes the unlikely means of Israel's deliverance, a minor but real echo of how God repeatedly uses the overlooked and the foreign, Rahab, Ruth, Naaman's servant girl, to advance His purposes for His people. Later Scripture never cites this chapter directly, but its themes, strength found in the LORD amid total loss and grace extended beyond strict merit, recur throughout the Psalms David is credited with writing and reach their fullest statement in the New Testament's teaching on grace.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The author wants readers to see David's fitness for kingship proven not in a battle he need not have fought at all had his own earlier choices not led him to Ziklag's undefended position, but in how he responds once catastrophe strikes, not with panic, not with self-justification against the men who blame him, but by seeking the LORD's strength first and then His explicit direction before acting. This is written to contrast David sharply with Saul, who in the previous stretch of chapters sought a medium rather than the LORD, 1 Samuel 28:6-7. The narrator also wants the equal sharing ruling remembered as David's own settled law, not an improvised kindness, framing it with the formal language of statute and ordinance, verse 25, so that later Israel would know its origin and its binding, permanent character. Finally, by ending with gifts distributed across Judah's towns, the author quietly explains, without stating it outright, how David had already built the goodwill that would make Judah's elders willing to crown him within the year.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The narrative describes what David actually decided in one particular crisis; it does not hand modern readers a fixed formula for dividing wages, spoils, or credit in every situation. What does carry forward as a binding principle, because the text itself frames it as a lasting statute rather than a passing mercy, is that those who serve in support roles, unable for whatever reason, exhaustion, illness, assignment, to stand on the front line, are not thereby lesser partners in a shared victory. The chapter is also descriptive rather than prescriptive about method, it does not command believers to consult an ephod, an instrument tied to Israel's priesthood that ceased with the temple; the abiding pattern is simply that believers ought to seek the LORD's guidance deliberately, by whatever means He has since given, rather than presuming to know His will or acting on raw emotion alone.

debates.question: Were David's men right to speak of stoning him?

views.label: Understandable grief turned to blame
views.case: Their sons and daughters were gone, and grief curdled into scapegoating the leader whose choices had left the town undefended.

views.label: A real threat to David's life and leadership
views.case: The text states plainly they spoke of stoning him, a genuine mutinous threat rather than mere venting, showing how fragile human loyalty is under pressure.

debates.bearing: Either way, the verse magnifies verse 6, with no human support left, David's only recourse was God Himself, and that is exactly where he turned.

debates.question: Was excluding the two hundred who stayed at the brook a reasonable proposal?

views.label: A natural, merit based instinct
views.case: Those who fought and risked their lives naturally felt the spoil should reward the risk they alone had taken.

views.label: A wicked distortion, by the text's own verdict
views.case: The narrator calls the men who proposed it wicked and worthless, showing the narrative itself rejects merit based exclusion of the weary as ungodly.

debates.bearing: David's ruling settles the question emphatically for Israel, victory won by the LORD is not to be rationed by human merit.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's two key verbs govern its shape. In verse 6, at the point of total loss, chazaq describes David strengthening himself, or being strengthened, in the LORD his God, a verb elsewhere used of taking firm hold, prevailing, standing fast, the opposite of collapse. In verse 8 darash describes David's inquiry of the LORD through the ephod, the same verb used of seeking a prophet, seeking God in worship, or diligently searching Him out; David does not presume divine favor but actively seeks it before he moves. Together the two verbs describe a man who, when every human prop is gone, both draws strength from God and asks direction from God, and only then acts.

Beyond these two, the chapter's account of the rescued Egyptian turns on a small but telling detail. He is revived, verse 12, with a piece of a fig cake and two clusters of raisins after three days without food or water, and the very next verse has David asking to whom do you belong, treating a starving foreign slave with the same courteous inquiry he will soon direct to the LORD Himself. The narrative pace slows here noticeably, three whole verses given to feeding one abandoned man, a deliberate delay that lets the reader feel how much this single act of ordinary kindness will end up costing, or rather paying, since this same man becomes the entire means of Israel's deliverance.

The dispute over sharing turns on the word cheleq, portion or share, used twice in David's ruling, the share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies, verse 24, the identical root the LORD uses to tell Aaron I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites, Numbers 18:20, and the same root behind a rebel's later boast that Israel has no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse's son, 2 Samuel 20:1. Applying the very word elsewhere reserved for one's stake in the LORD or in the king himself to a simple division of plunder quietly elevates the whole dispute, this is not haggling over goods but a question of who truly belongs to the community and its blessings. The pairing of statute and ordinance, choq and mishpat, verse 25, are two distinct Hebrew legal terms for fixed law, used together elsewhere for the most solemn, permanent obligations Israel receives, so that David's decision is deliberately clothed in the vocabulary Israel used for its most binding commands, not offered merely as a personal preference that later leaders might quietly set aside.

typology.type: David recovering all that was lost to the raiders
typology.fulfillment: Not one person or possession is left behind, verses 18-19 insist on this twice, nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder. This total, exhaustive recovery anticipates Christ's own promise concerning those the Father has given Him, that He will lose none of them but raise them up on the last day, John 6:39, and that no one will snatch them from His hand, John 10:28. Where David's recovery was won by force of arms against a real enemy, Christ's is won by His own death and resurrection against sin and death themselves, a costlier and more complete victory.

typology.type: David's equal sharing of the plunder with the weary who stayed behind
typology.fulfillment: Against men who wanted a merit based division, all fight, all share only among the fighters, David insists they will share alike, verse 24, so that endurance and exhaustion receive the same reward as valor and violence. The parable of the workers hired at different hours yet paid the identical wage pictures the same logic in Christ's kingdom, where reward flows from the master's generosity rather than from the precise measure of a worker's exertion, Matthew 20:1-16. David's ruling and Christ's parable both unsettle a purely transactional view of reward, replacing it with grace distributed by the giver's character rather than the receiver's output.

typology.type: The unnamed Egyptian slave, rescued though half dead, who becomes the means of victory
typology.fulfillment: An outsider, enslaved, abandoned by his own master to die in a field, verse 13, is revived with bread and water and becomes the very means by which Israel's captives are found and rescued. It is a small but real picture of how God works through the lowest and the overlooked, an Egyptian rather than an Israelite, a slave rather than a soldier, to accomplish deliverance, the same pattern by which Christ, despised and without stately form, Isaiah 53:2-3, becomes the one through whom rescue actually comes to those who could not save themselves.

typology.type: David found strength in the LORD at the point of total loss
typology.fulfillment: Stripped of home, family, and the loyalty of his own men, who spoke of stoning him, verse 6, David's only recourse becomes the LORD Himself, and out of that low point comes total victory. Paul later learns that God's power is perfected in weakness, 2 Corinthians 12:9, and Christ Himself, having nothing and no one left in Gethsemane, His own disciples asleep and about to scatter, presses on in obedience to the Father's will, Matthew 26:39-42, the same pattern of strength found only when every other support has failed.

study.christ:
David at Ziklag is stripped of everything a king needs, home, family, and the confidence of his own men, some of whom speak openly of stoning him, verse 6. He has no army to command in the ordinary sense, only grief stricken fathers ready to turn on their leader. Yet it is at this precise low point, with every human prop removed, that David turns wholly to the LORD and finds there the strength that carries him to total victory. This anticipates the far deeper humiliation of great David's greater Son, who was likewise stripped of everything, His clothing divided by lot, His closest friends asleep or fled, His own cry from the cross naming a felt abandonment, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, Matthew 27:46, and who was nonetheless raised by the Father's power to a victory infinitely larger than David's recovered flocks and family.

The recovery itself is total, nothing was missing, verses 18-19 declare twice over, an emphasis that finds its fulfillment in Christ's promise that He will lose none of those the Father has given Him, John 6:39, and that His sheep will never perish, John 10:28. David's victory over the Amalekites recovers what an enemy had stolen, Christ's victory over sin and death recovers everyone the Father has entrusted to Him, and does so completely, without exception, exactly as David's own men found nothing missing when the fighting ended.

The sharing of the plunder deepens the parallel further. David could have let the weary two hundred go empty handed, and some of his own men wanted exactly that, but he ruled that the one who stayed with the supplies would share equally with the one who fought, verse 24, establishing it as permanent law for Israel. Christ's kingdom operates by the same logic of grace rather than merit, the workers hired at the eleventh hour receive the same wage as those who bore the day's heat, Matthew 20:1-16, and no disciple's reward in His kingdom is finally rationed by how much they were able to contribute. As David turned personal recovery into shared blessing for the exhausted and even for distant towns in Judah, so Christ turns His own finished victory into an inheritance freely shared with those who could never have won it for themselves.
study.god:
God does not prevent Ziklag from burning. The text gives no warning, no rescue before the fact, only the ashes David and his men find on the third day, verse 3. This is a God who permits real loss, even to His anointed, rather than shielding him from every consequence of his own choices, since it was David's absence at the Philistine muster, itself the fruit of his earlier decision to dwell among Israel's enemies, 1 Samuel 27, that left Ziklag undefended in the first place. Yet the same God meets David precisely inside that loss rather than only after it, and the verb the text uses, David found strength in the LORD his God, verse 6, describes an active, reaching faith rather than a passive comfort that simply arrives.

God also answers plainly when sought. David does not receive a vague impression or a delayed silence, he inquires through the ephod and receives a direct command and a direct promise in the same breath, pursue, you will surely overtake, you will rescue, verse 8. This immediacy contrasts sharply with the silence Saul had met from the LORD only two chapters earlier, by dream, by Urim, or by prophets, 1 Samuel 28:6, a silence that drove Saul to a medium instead. The same God who has gone quiet toward a disobedient king speaks clearly to an obedient one, not because David is sinless, but because he actually asks, and keeps asking, rather than presuming or despairing.

Finally, God's character of grace becomes fixed law through David's own ruling. The statute that the one who stayed with the supplies shares equally with the one who fought, verses 24-25, is presented as something David establishes, yet the text frames the entire recovery as what the LORD has given, verse 23, so the sharing itself becomes an act of worship, distributing God's gift the way God's own character would distribute it. A God who gives freely to those who did not earn the victory shapes a king who gives freely to those who could not fully share the fight, and that shape, once fixed as ordinance, outlives David himself, binding Israel to God's own generosity long after this single battle is forgotten.

crossReferences.note: Moses instructs that plunder from a holy war be divided evenly between the soldiers who fought and the rest of the congregation who did not, the Mosaic precedent David extends into permanent law when he rules that those who stayed with the supplies share alike with those who pursued the Amalekites.

The LORD gives strength to the weary and renews the strength of those who wait on Him, so they run and do not grow weary, a promise that reads like a commentary on David's own experience at Ziklag, where the man who had no strength left to weep, verse 4, was strengthened instead by the LORD.

David elsewhere confesses that the LORD is his strength and his fortress, the God who arms him with strength, language that likely grew out of exactly this kind of crisis, when every human source of security, home, family, the loyalty of his men, had failed him at once.

The workers hired at the eleventh hour receive the same wage as those who labored all day, a parable of grace that pictures the same logic behind David's ruling that the one who stayed with the supplies shares equally with the one who fought and won.

Achish had given Ziklag to David as his own possession during his time among the Philistines, the very town whose destruction, while David's forces were away at the Philistine muster, sets this whole chapter of loss and recovery in motion.

Saul had been commanded to destroy the Amalekites completely and failed to carry it out, sparing king Agag and the best of the plunder, the disobedience that cost him his kingdom; David's total victory here, sparing nothing of the enemy's gain, stands in silent contrast to that earlier failure.

Moses commands Israel to remember what Amalek did on the journey from Egypt and to blot out its memory from under heaven once settled in the land, the standing sentence against Amalek that both Saul's campaign and David's pursuit here carry out, however incompletely, generations later.

Soon after this chapter the men of Judah anoint David king at Hebron, one of the very towns named among those that received a gift of plunder from Ziklag, verse 31, showing how David's generosity here quietly prepared the ground for his coronation.

Amalek first attacked Israel from behind on the journey out of Egypt, striking the weak and straggling, an old pattern of raiding the vulnerable that resurfaces almost unchanged when Amalekite raiders strike Ziklag while David's strongest men are away at the Philistine muster.

Paul learns that God's power is perfected in weakness, so he can be content with hardships for Christ's sake, for when I am weak, then I am strong, the same paradox David lives out when his own total weakness at Ziklag becomes the very place he finds strength in God.

study.oneStory:
David's rock bottom moment at Ziklag, home burned, wives and children gone, his own men speaking openly of stoning him, sits near the very end of his long fugitive years, the last recorded crisis before news of Saul's death changes everything. It is one of Scripture's starkest pictures of a person stripped down to nothing, and it becomes, precisely because of that stripping, one of Scripture's clearest pictures of finding strength in God alone rather than in circumstance, reputation, or the loyalty of others, all of which David has just lost in a single day.

The chapter's movement, from ashes to inquiry to total recovery to generous sharing, mirrors in miniature the whole shape of the biblical story, catastrophe met not with despair but with a turning to God, a clear word received, decisive action taken, complete restoration granted, and then that restoration extended as grace to those who could not fully share in winning it. Israel's own history runs the same arc across centuries, exile met with a promised return, loss answered by a greater inheritance than what was lost.

David's insistence that the exhausted two hundred share equally in the spoil becomes, in miniature, a preview of grace as it will be defined in the New Testament, given by the giver's character rather than measured by the receiver's output. And the gifts sent afterward to a dozen towns in Judah, unglamorous, almost bureaucratic in their listing, quietly begin building the kingdom that God had already promised David, a kingdom he receives not by grasping for the crown at Saul's death but by generosity long before anyone offers it to him.

The chapter closes one story, David's years as a hunted fugitive, even as it opens another, and stands as one more link in the long chain by which God restores what sin and circumstance destroy and shares that restoration freely, a chain that reaches its full length in Christ, the true King who recovers everything lost and gives it to His people as sheer gift.

quiz.q: What did David do when his own men spoke of stoning him after Ziklag was burned?

options.text: He found strength in the LORD his God, turning to God rather than to despair or retaliation.
options.note: Verse 6 states this plainly as David's response at his lowest point.

options.text: He immediately organized the men into search parties.
options.note: Pursuit did follow soon after, but the text specifically credits his first response as finding strength in the LORD.

options.text: He fled from his men to save himself.
options.note: The text says nothing of David fleeing; he stayed and turned to God.

options.text: He gave in and let the men stone him.
options.note: David was not stoned; strengthened by God, he led the recovery.

quiz.q: Before pursuing the raiders, what did David do?

options.text: He inquired of the LORD through the ephod, asking whether to pursue and whether he would succeed.
options.note: Verses 7-8 show David seeking explicit divine guidance before acting.

options.text: He counted his men and assessed their strength.
options.note: The exhaustion of two hundred men is noted during the pursuit, but the initiating step was inquiry of the LORD, not a headcount.

options.text: He consulted the elders of Judah first.
options.note: No such consultation is recorded before the pursuit.

options.text: He acted immediately without seeking any guidance.
options.note: This contradicts the text; David explicitly inquired of the LORD first.

quiz.q: How did David's men find the Amalekite camp?

options.text: An abandoned, half dead Egyptian slave, revived by David's men, led them to the raiders.
options.note: Verses 11-16 describe the Egyptian's rescue and his role as guide.

options.text: David tracked footprints in the sand himself.
options.note: No such detail appears; the Egyptian guide is the means given in the text.

options.text: A prophet directed them by a vision.
options.note: No prophet or vision is mentioned in this account, only the ephod inquiry and the Egyptian guide.

options.text: They found the camp by pure chance with no help.
options.note: The text explicitly credits the rescued Egyptian slave as the guide.

quiz.q: What happened to everything the Amalekites had taken from Ziklag?

options.text: David recovered everything and everyone; nothing was missing.
options.note: Verses 18-19 state plainly that nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any plunder.

options.text: David recovered most of the people but lost some of the plunder.
options.note: The text is emphatic that nothing at all was missing, not a partial recovery.

options.text: Only the wives were recovered; the rest of the plunder was lost.
options.note: The recovery included the wives and everyone and everything else taken.

options.text: The Amalekites escaped with everything.
options.note: The opposite is true; David struck them down and recovered all.

quiz.q: When some men wanted to exclude the two hundred who stayed at the Brook of Besor from the plunder, what did David rule?

options.text: That the share of the one who stayed with the supplies would match the share of the one who went to battle, share alike, and this became a lasting statute.
options.note: Verses 23-25 record David's ruling and its establishment as ongoing law in Israel.

options.text: That the two hundred should receive a smaller share as compensation for not fighting.
options.note: David ruled for an equal share, not a reduced one.

options.text: That the decision would be left to each soldier individually.
options.note: David issued a binding ruling himself, not a matter of individual choice.

options.text: That David agreed with the wicked men and excluded the two hundred.
options.note: David rebuked this proposal and ruled the opposite way.

quiz.q: What did David do with some of the recovered plunder after returning to Ziklag?

options.text: He sent gifts to the elders of Judah and various towns, calling it a gift from the plunder of the LORD's enemies.
options.note: Verses 26-31 list the towns to which David sent gifts from the plunder.

options.text: He kept it all for his own men only.
options.note: David deliberately extended the gift beyond his own men to the wider towns of Judah.

options.text: He returned it to the Amalekites as a peace offering.
options.note: There is no return of plunder to the enemy; it was distributed as gifts to Judah.

options.text: He destroyed the plunder as devoted to the LORD.
options.note: The plunder was distributed as gifts, not destroyed.

questions: David found strength in the LORD when he had lost everything and even his own men turned against him. Where in your life right now do you need to seek strength in God rather than in people or circumstances that may fail you?
Before acting, David paused to inquire of the LORD rather than assuming what to do. What decision are you facing where you need to slow down and seek God's direction first?
Some of David's men wanted to withhold reward from those who were too weary to fight. Where are you tempted to measure others' worth by their visible output rather than extending grace?
David turned personal recovery into shared blessing, for his men and even for distant towns in Judah. How generous are you with what God restores to you?
The whole recovery began with rescuing a forgotten, half dead foreign slave. How does God's use of the overlooked and weak challenge how you view usefulness in his plans?

translationNotes.note: Found strength renders the Hebrew chazaq, sometimes translated strengthened himself; the reflexive sense stresses David's active reliance on God rather than passive comfort.
Inquired renders darash, the standard verb for consulting the LORD, here through the priestly ephod Abiathar brought; some English versions render the same root as sought.
Statute and ordinance translates two closely related Hebrew legal terms paired for emphasis, underscoring that David's ruling became fixed, lasting law in Israel, not a one time favor.
